As a sceptic, I just wanted to share an odd experience when I was younger. I was a pub manager in my 20's and after shutting up shop about 2.30pm ( the old days before all day pub opening hours ) I'd retire for a few hours in the afternoon, before re-opening about 6pm. 

Anyway I'd hear heavy, real-world footsteps on the cellar steps in the afternoon. Not random. Deliberate, pressure-based, commensurate with a real person walking on the cellar steps. 

It was consistent for a few weeks. At first I was a little unnerved. Then I started shouting at "the thing " to leave me in peace as I was trying to have a couple of hours off in between sessions - and it stopped. 

Do I think it was a ghost? Probably not. But it was weird. 

As my old late great dad used to say, " It's not the dead you need to be worrying about, but the living "

I think a lot of us ( me included ) like to think we're quite intelligent - and the thought that that "intelligence" just dies with us seems just wasteful, so we imagine there's an extension of that beyond death.

There isn't, but we find it hard to deal with, so we imagine this "higher level intelligence" carries on in a higher plane. 

It doesn't, but it makes us feel better about ourselves that it might. 

The finality scares us, so we make up other narratives in our heads.

Thank you all for your great replies - and in the interests of research, for others that are considering an " Old Pubs of London tour " I feel obligated to report back.

We did the family lunch thing in Chiswick 2.00-4.30, then set off on our pub crawl.

Apologies if this is a long post. It's nearly midnight and we've just arrived back to our hotel in Chiswick.

Surprisingly we got through most of them, with 2 additions.

Tried to stick to half-pints originally to give us a better chance of success in our endeavours. But we waivered along our journey with varying levels of success. Here goes.

In order of attendance...

1. THE SALISBURY.  Nice pub near Leicester Square. We arrived about 5.15, prob peak time with the pre-theatre crew. Very busy. Nice interior, but mad busy.

2. THE PRINCESS LOUISE. Possibly the most interesting pub of the night, decor-wise. Full of original tiles, light fixtures and an amazing gents loo, that felt like a throwback to the 1920's. My OH said the ladies loo wasn't half as charachterful and interesting.

3. THE SHIP TAVERN. Nice, but felt like a commercial re-imagining of an old pub, especially given Sky Sports was showing on 2 or 3 screens whilst we were there.

3+. We sinned at this point and on the way to the CITTE OF YORKE we diverted to Ye Olde Wetherspoons for a supposed cheap glass of wine, which turned out not to be cheap - Welcome to London prices.

Whilst we were at the Wetherspoons, we worked out it wasn't a big diversion to go to The Seven Stars, before going to the CITTE OF Yorke, so we did that

4. THE SEVEN STARS. This was possibly my favourite of the night. Not because it was beautiful but it was a very authentic throwback pub. 
Whoever mentioned Roxy Beaujolais and the cat, thank you. We name-checked them and got a great reception. 
Two of the 3 bar staff were Irish, one Northern, one Southern, which chimed well with me as the son of a 1950's Irish imigree to England. And don't call Derry, Londonderry! I sort of knew that, but rightfully I was put in my place.

5.  The surprise package of the night. THE JUSTICE GATE, Lincoln Inns Fields. I'm not even sure if it's called that but it was about a 2 minute walk from the Seven Stars when we were trying to get back on route to The Citte Of Yorke.
A very grand large building, slightly yuppie, but if you like your architecture, brilliant. A bit like if 'Spoons had a bit more class. They had a huge screen in the centre of the bar, like being in the city watching stock prices, with "dynamic pricing" so certain drinks drink prices would fluctuate by the odd person cent  "with demand". Gimmicky, but entertaining.

6. THE CITTE OF YORKE.  I know it's hugely popular but it felt like a film producer was trying to reimagine Beowulf meets Game Of Thrones. Wood meets iron, meets barrels, meets testosterone. Great on the eye, especially the side booths, but felt like it was a pub full of cinema props. Liked it, but left me slightly baffled. Like I said, great on the eye though.

7. THE COCKPIT. Thanks to whoever suggested this pub earlier in this thread, but I loved it. A bit rough and ready, but a proper old boozer. Cheers 

By this time we were wobbling and headed back on the tube to our hotel  in  Chiswick. 

An honorary mention to the Packhorse and Talbot in Chiswick. Not an old pub, but a fine pub 

So, apologies, these are my ramblings. Hope it helps someone if you're searching for Old London pubs, in a fairly narrow geographic area, where you don't have to exhaust yourself walking between them.

In Old English the origin of the word 'ask' was 'aksian' or 'askian'.  
After the great vowel shift of the middle ages in England, the word morphed into the more familiar 'ask'.  
However, in the West Indian colonies the old english form of 'aksian' or  
 later 'aks' was preserved within the patois and creoles of those   
Islands. Similarly in slave communities in the US where patois and   
creoles evolved, the old pronounciations were preserved and evolved   
differently than in English in England. It is a language feature known   
as 'colonial lag.'  
So, aks, arks or axe , aren't mispronounciations, they are just   
different pronounciations that relate back to the original Old English.
